references.text: Also in the Acts of the Apostles, the listeners become furious when they hear the apostles' testimony. The words "they were stirred up" show the same reaction of anger as in the synagogue at Nazareth.

When Stephen spoke about Israel's disobedience and accused the people, they became furious (ἐθυμοῦντο) and drove him out of the city to stone him – a very parallel sequence of events to what Jesus experienced in Nazareth.

Earlier in the same story, the people were amazed and positive, but when Jesus began to speak about God's grace also applying to Gentiles, the mood turned to rage – this verse provides the context for the sudden anger.
The scribes and Pharisees became filled with rage (ἀνοίας) when Jesus healed on the Sabbath – once again, religious leaders react with anger when Jesus challenges their expectations.

When the Jews in Antioch of Pisidia saw that Gentiles were flocking to hear Paul, they became full of envy and contradicted him – similar resistance to what Jesus faced when he mentioned God's blessings toward Gentiles.

Naaman from Syria became furious when the prophet Elisha did not meet with him personally, yet was still healed – this is one of the stories Jesus referred to just before the crowd became angry, since Elisha helped a Gentile.
Elijah was sent to the widow in Zarephath, a Gentile – the second story Jesus mentioned that provoked rage, because it showed that God's prophets were sent to Gentiles rather than Israel.
Proverbs says that mockers stir up a city, which is reflected in the violent reaction of the crowd in the synagogue at Nazareth.
Also in John's Gospel, the crowd tries to stone Jesus after he said something that deeply provoked them – a similar pattern where Jesus' words lead to violent rage.
